https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Grant Shapps: ‘Labour is now the political wing of Just Stop Oil’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: Energy policy will be one of the great dividing lines between Labour and the Conservatives at the next election – but Grant Shapps is upbeat
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Grant Shapps has a one-word distillation for Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer’s proposal to ban new licences for oil and gas drilling if he wins power next year: “Bonkers.”
“I think actually their energy policy represents a clear and present danger to national security, as simple as that,” says Shapps. “I think the Labour Party in some sense has become the political wing of Just Stop Oil. They have taken money from one of the same funders.”
The reference is to Dale Vince, who founded the green energy firm Ecotricity, donated £1.5 million to Labour and has joined protests with the climate change group Just Stop Oil.
The licences policy, says Shapps, “is one of those things where I’m sure in Islington it sounded like a really good idea, but is fundamentally crazy and dangerous”.
He adds: “It’s crazy, because we can’t just stop using hydrocarbons and even the Committee for Climate Change says we’ll still be using some in 2050. If you decide to just stop extracting them, you’re going to have to bring them in from somewhere and you’ll bring them in with twice the carbon, so totally self-defeating.
“You potentially destroy 140,000 jobs in the process and you hand the power to dictators like [Vladimir] Putin. So it is really like a wholesale surrender of our energy policy. It puts the country in danger from a security perspective. It’s naive. Even the unions call it naive.”
The Labour position is a little more nuanced than the simple distillation suggests. The key word is “new”. Only new licences for drilling would be blocked by Sir Keir. Existing licences will not be scrapped, Labour has made clear. So wells already running in the North Sea would still keep operating, meaning some would be extracting for two or three more decades to come.
Yet the policy difference is real. Saying “no more” to new drilling would be a significant moment, a drawing of the line under Britain’s oil and gas industry in the long-run. It is a flash point in a wider debate, one playing out not just in Britain but across the world – how to stop potentially catastrophic global warming and deal with its impacts.
Both the Conservatives and Labour are publicly committed to making the UK a “net zero” carbon emitter by 2050, a target enshrined into law under Theresa May. The differences come over how far and how fast to reach for that target, as well as what degree of financial pain should be passed onto households in the process.
Labour accuses the Tories of just paying lip service to the target, not taking the politically tricky short-term decisions needed to bring about that reality by 2050. The Tories in turn accuse their rivals of putting climate change ideology over the immediate economic needs of the country, being too willing to risk jobs on the switch.
Is the truth not that in unpicking a century and a half of industrial revolution and pivoting to a non-carbon economy, it is inevitable there will be huge costs for British families? “No, no. No, I don’t think that’s right at all,” says Shapps, waving away the suggestion – despite having minutes earlier linked Labour’s policy to the UK’s current inflation problem, and argued that in future the approach could raise prices by limiting supply.
“The way I see my job is written on here, energy security and net zero,” he adds, picking up the embossed folder lying on the desk with the title on it. “Two sides of the same coin. If you ask me what I think my first job is, it’s energy security, right? It is making sure the British people have a plentiful supply of energy.
“Prices are now going to start coming down from next month. I want to see us with the cheapest electricity prices in Europe, amongst the cheapest by the middle of the next decade. And I can only do that if I make this change in the way that we produce our energy sensibly.”
Shapps is typically enthusiastic about his new role, which he took on in February, jumping from being Rishi Sunak’s business secretary to head of the newly created Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. He is, in fact, one of the great ministerial survivors from this long Conservative run in Downing Street, which stretches back to 2010 and covers five different prime ministers.
He was on the frontbenches from week one of David Cameron’s premiership as housing minister, rising to the role of Conservative Party chairman, but was then culled from cabinet after the 2015 election win. Under Theresa May there was time in the wilderness of the backbench, with Shapps becoming one of the most prominent Tory voices calling for her to go, before a cabinet return under Boris Johnson, being given the role of transport secretary.
Another demotion came under Liz Truss before a shock return, spending six days as home secretary as Truss teetered then fell, sliding from there into Sunak’s cabinet.It means Shapps, 54, is theoretically caught between loyalties – to Johnson, who returned him to the cabinet, and Sunak, his current political master.
The enmity between those two men is no secret. Johnsonites blame Sunak for bringing him down. Sunak quit as chancellor last July and triggered a rush to the door from other ministers which meant Boris’s time was up. So, if Johnson, now no longer an MP, wants to be a Tory candidate in a new seat for next year’s election, would Shapps be supportive?
“Look, all those matters would be for the party,” he replies, apparently wary of talking up the return of a man who has proved such a thorn in the side of the current Tory leader. “I don’t think even Boris thinks he’s about to stand for a seat at the next election though,” he adds – a conclusion that chimes with those around Johnson. Though others, including Truss, have cautioned against ruling out his comeback.
Shapps avoided another Boris-shaped headache this week, finding himself absent from a vote on the privileges committee partygate report that found Johnson had repeatedly and deliberately misled MPs over lockdown-breaking parties in No 10. The House of Commons approved the report, meaning Johnson was stripped of his parliamentary pass – something never before done to a former prime minister – but scores of Tories did not cast ballots, including Shapps.
So, does Shapps agree with the report? His response walks the tightrope: “We set these things up. We may not like what they say. And, by the way, I think it’s perfectly proper that people are allowed to criticise what a report says. That in itself is democracy.
“But, in the end, a process is put in place. There have been far too many column inches wasted going round and round in circles and so I don’t think there’s anything valuable I can really add to it.”
Shapps has built a reputation as an effective media communicator. His videos while transport secretary, one featuring a cameo from Tory-grandee-turned-TV-presenter Michael Portillo at a train station, are now being copied by other Cabinet ministers.
He is also known for his number-crunching. Since the Theresa May rebellion days, Shapps has been keeping an electronic spreadsheet detailing every Tory MP’s past votes and positions in an attempt to accurately predict how key votes will play out. It was used to help propel Johnson into the premiership in 2019 and keep him there when colleagues began to turn. Shapps predicted the result of the no confidence ballot in Johnson last June among Tory MPs to within a single vote using the system.
So, as keeper of the spreadsheet and with the Conservatives 17 percentage points behind Labour in the opinion poll averages, how is the mood among Tory MPs right now?
“Well, look, as you often find in mid-Parliament you can be going through really tough times,” says Shapps. “We’ve had with Covid, with the war in Ukraine, and with some problems brought upon ourselves in fairness, some unbelievably difficult times.
“On the other hand, we’ve now got leadership with Rishi which is solid and sound. [His] five priorities, I think, really match with your readers’ priorities. Stopping the small boats, growing the economy – these are fundamentally important missions. And I think most people actually also realise that what Rishi brings to the table is the ability to solve problems.”
He cites the deal to ease post-Brexit trade between Northern Ireland and the rest of the UK – the Windsor Framework – which was agreed in February. “Lots of people, lots of commentators were telling us it was impossible to solve and [Sunak] has the attention to detail to do that,” he says.
The Prime Minister will need every ounce of his problem-solving skills to meet one of the Government’s most ambitious policies: the phasing out of all petrol and diesel cars and vans in favour of electric vehicles. Shapps, it transpires, is an EV evangelist. “They are spectacular,” he says. “When you change gears you have the same pull throughout.
“They are fantastic. I want to make [the transition to electric] comfortable. I do not believe in doing it in a way which destroys our energy security or doing it in a way which costs British families money. I want to focus on the security side.” The praise for electric vehicles comes from first-hand experience. Shapps is already on his second Tesla.
What about the high price of EVs, and the current concerns about Britain’s public charging infrastructure? He says he is confident prices will come down. “They should end up being cheaper because there are 20,000 moving parts in an internal combustion engine vehicle and about 200 moving parts in an electric vehicle. So, in many ways, they’re much more simple.”
Some 70 per cent of Britons have driveways or off-street parking, Shapps adds, so if the Government really can put in place the charging infrastructure – a big if – then there is the opportunity for wider pick-up.
An encouraging sign that the Government is capable of putting its money where its mouth is when it comes to protecting households from the financial cost of net zero is the way it has approached the issue of hydrogen. As a carbon and methane-free gas, hydrogen is seen as critical as Britain weans itself off more polluting energy sources. Like a lot of emerging, cleaner energy forms, the Government is committed to helping build the industry by providing financial support.
The question, as always, is where the money comes from. Ministers had proposed a “hydrogen levy”, the idea being that a little extra be added on to energy bills – as had been done for years for other green energy forms. But in recent weeks, a Conservative rebellion has emerged over the proposal, which is included in the Energy Bill making its way through Parliament.
Shapps had previously indicated his nervousness about the move, but is now prepared to be explicit: he does not want the levy put directly onto household bills. He says: “What we need to do is make sure, A, we can get our hydrogen industry up and running. Really, really important, massive export opportunities, great way to store energy, great way to power heavy industry and what have you. And, B, I don’t want to see people’s household bills unnecessarily bashed by this.”
Pushed for clarification, Shapps hardens the line: “We know we need to fund this transition, but we don’t want to do it through household levies.” He also talks up the potential for nuclear power to bring about Britain’s cleaner, greener future. Shapps visited Hinkley Point C recently, the next big nuclear power plant due to come online.
He says: “The reactor itself at Hinkley Point will be the world’s most powerful nuclear reactor in terms of energy produced. So this country that built Calder Hall in Cumbria in 1953 and became the world’s first country to have civil nuclear power, is about to have the world’s most powerful nuclear reactor in terms of electricity produced.”
Sizewell C will follow Hinkley. Small nuclear reactors will also be part of the mix, says Shapps. “We have many great nuclear small modular reactor companies in this country doing lots of really interesting things. At the large end, Rolls Royce, which has been running effectively small modular reactors in nuclear subs for decades under the sea, is a world leader. And we’ve got many other smaller firms as well. So I think there is an enormous opportunity for this country to take a lead and every country wants this stuff.”
Energy policy looks set to be one of the great dividing lines between Labour and the Conservatives at the next election. And unsurprisingly, Shapps, the Tories’ great cheerleader, is upbeat, in general, about his party’s chances. Downing Street says it is convinced the polls – which have closed since Sunak took over from Truss – will be even tighter come the next election, due at some point in 2024, most likely in the autumn.
Some Tory MPs privately fear a 1997-style wipeout could be on the way, but Shapps doesn’t agree.
“I very much look forward to that being a 1992 or 2015 moment, actually, if we’re going to go back to history,” he responds. The first was when Neil Kinnock’s “We’re alright!” declaration at a rally just before the election proved illusory, John Major’s Tories beating Labour again, while the latter saw David Cameron escape from the shackles of the Coalition with a new Tory majority.
“Of course, no one can accurately predict exactly what will happen. I’m not saying we will win, I’m saying we can win,” says Shapps.
Time is running out to turn the possible into the probable.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.title: Watch: Motorcyclist rams past Just Stop Oil protesters
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.subtitle: Driver revs his engine and edges into activists’ banner before speeding past them during a protest on the A12 in London
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.text:
A motorcyclist refused to be stopped by Just Stop Oil protesters on Monday morning, ploughing through their demonstration in London.
The environmental group attempted to block two lanes of traffic on the A12 at Gants Hill shortly after 8.30am, but faced the wrath of motorists before police ordered them to leave half an hour later.’
The motorcyclist revved his engine and edged into the activists’ orange banner, before finding a gap to hurtle through and accelerate away.
Video footage of the encounter shows activists clinging to the rider’s arms in a desperate attempt to stop him passing.
Multiple drivers and a cyclist were also seen snatching the group’s banners away, while queues of gridlocked vehicles sounded their horns.
A mother also shouted at the protesters, saying “I need to get my kids to school”, having said she just dropped them off on a bus that was stuck in the tailbacks.
It was the latest in a series of protests by the climate group that have resulted in tensions boiling over. The group’s campaign of “slow marches” along arterial roads in the capital is now in its seventh week.
Just Stop Oil has vowed to continue its campaign “indefinitely” until the Government commits to its demand of halting any new licences for fossil fuel extraction.
Just Stop Oil claimed that 75 supporters marched through four locations in the capital on Monday morning, including “a team led by eight health professionals”.
One of the doctors said through a megaphone: “My name is Hillary, I’m a GP, I’m here today in support of Just Stop Oil because as a doctor I have a professional duty to protect the health of my patients and the public and to keep children safe.
“But the public and particularly children are not safe; the temperatures are rising, climate change is advancing and we’re facing a crisis.
“We are already at risk; millions are already dying across the world and in the UK of heat and drought and more will come.”
The Metropolitan Police said regarding the A12 protest: “Officers imposed Section 12 conditions on those involved at 08:56hrs. Within two minutes the road was cleared.”
On a separate protest, it said: “At 08:03hrs, Monday 5 June, we were notified of Just Stop Oil protesters walking slowly in the road along the A13.
“We arrived on scene at 08:19hrs and Section 12 conditions were issued on those involved at 08.20hrs. The road was cleared at 08:26hrs.”
Police added that they attended another slow march on Kennington Lane, south London, where two Just Stop Oil supporters were arrested shortly after police issued a Section 12 notice, including a 24-year-old physics graduate.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Labour hires former Extinction Rebellion lawyer as climate and energy adviser
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: Tobias Garnett led the group in a landmark case that resulted in lifting of ban on its London protests and charges against thousands dropped
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Labour has hired Extinction Rebellion’s former top lawyer who represented the activists who shut down roads near Parliament.
Tobias Garnett led the environmental group in a landmark court case that saw the lifting of a ban on its protests in London and charges against thousands of protestors dropped.
But two months later, he was headhunted to become the Labour Party’s climate and energy political adviser and now works for Ed Miliband, the shadow secretary of state for climate change and net zero.
Conservative MPs said it proves there is a “revolving door between eco-extremists and Labour HQ”.
Mr Garnett coordinated Extinction Rebellion’s legal strategy team as a human rights lawyer in 2019, admitting in an article for The Guardian at the time that its protests were illegal but defended them as “a desperate attempt to jolt politicians out of their inertia”.
He led the group in a crucial High Court ruling that ruled the Metropolitan Police’s ban on the activists’ protests was unlawful after they shut down roads around Parliament, superglued themselves to a plane at London City Airport and sparked an outcry by jumping on Tube trains during rush hour.
It prompted Mr Garnett to tell television crews he was delighted at the victory, adding that the judgment “affirm[s] that when the people of this country assemble peacefully to demand action on the climate and ecological emergency the law is on our side”.
The ruling led to claims from Extinction Rebellion that around 1,000 police cases against its activists would be dropped.
Mr Garnett also criticised attempts to crack down on environmental protests as “wasting time and money” and boasted that “direct action like this may be justified to avert the greater damage that climate change promises”, warning of “eco-fascism forged in the crucible of scarce resources”.
But within a year, he had been poached by Labour in January 2020 to be a policy advisor on Sir Keir Starmer’s leadership campaign, before beginning his current rule as the party’s climate and energy guru.
He is now one of the most influential figures setting the party’s green agenda ahead of next year’s general election, including its recent pledge to stop handing out new oil and gas licences in the North Sea.
The revelation comes after it emerged last week that one of Labour’s biggest financial supporters, Dale Vince who has given more than £1.5 million to the party, also bankrolls the controversial eco group Just Stop Oil.
Lee Anderson, the deputy chair of the Conservative Party, told The Telegraph: “There should be no doubt whose tune Labour marches to. Their entire energy policy is being dictated by Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil loonies.
“As these eco-zealots line Starmer’s pockets with their donations and whisper in his ear, Labour are plotting to smash up British industry, kill thousands of jobs and leave us at the mercy of foreign powers.
“Labour’s policy is a surrender plan and these fanatics won’t rest until our energy security is completely dismantled.”
Andrea Jenkyns, another Tory MP who is on the board of directors of the campaign group Net Zero Watch, told The Telegraph: “This lays bare the frightening reality that the British public could expect under Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, fuelled by a revolving door between eco-extremists and Labour HQ.
“They are rubbing their hands with glee at the thought of tanking the economy in the pursuit of net zero, leaving ordinary working people to pay the price while they pander to their zealous paymasters.”
Labour was contacted for comment.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Lib Dem 'farmers' candidate' in Somerset by-election is pro-vegan Extinction Rebellion supporter
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: Sarah Dyke is promoted as someone who can give a voice to agriculturalists, but critics claim she backs reducing meat consumption
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
A Liberal Democrats candidate promoted as a farmer’s daughter who will understand rural needs has been attacked for promoting veganism and meeting with radical environmentalists.
Sarah Dyke was selected as the Lib Dems’ candidate for the seat of Somerset and Frome after its Tory MP was suspended over sexual harassment and cocaine allegations.
David Warburton triggered a by-election when he resigned as an MP on June 17.
He was elected as a Conservative but sat as an independent after losing the Conservative whip last year following allegations of sexual misconduct.
He apologised for using cocaine, but denied sexual misconduct.
Ms Dyke’s Lib Dem web page states: “Sarah lives in the constituency and is from a Somerset farming family which can be traced back over 250 years to the local area.”
But ahead of the election on July 20, there are now claims that Ms Dyke is a supporter of radical direct action environmental groups such as Extinction Rebellion and has backed calls for a reduction in meat consumption and a switch to plant-based diets.
Opponents say this stands in contrast to her self-promotion as a candidate sympathetic to farmers and rural communities.
Now Tories are branding her a “hardline eco-loon” in a bid to undermine her support.
The Conservatives have issued a “dossier” of material which they say exposes Ms Dyke as an extreme environmentalist.
It points out that the 51-year-old held meetings with Extinction Rebellion in 2019 to develop South Somerset Council’s environment strategy.
In March 2021 Ms Dyke also appeared at a Youth Environment Summit Somerset event featuring Extinction Rebellion campaigners Katie Hodgetts and Caroline Hickman.
She has taken part in road blockades and occupations and describes herself as someone her parents would call “a general nuisance”.
Ms Hickman was pictured at an Extinction Rebellion event in London which the Conservatives claim was “aimed at promoting climate extremism among young children”.
Her opponents also claim her online activity reveals that she stands at odds with the needs and interests of ordinary rural voters.
The dossier points out that her internet history shows she has previously “liked” a number of Facebook pages for radical climate groups such as Extinction Rebellion Somerset, Extinction Rebellion Bruton, Greenpeace, Green New Deal Rising, Green Alliance and Feminist Anarchist.
It also alleges Ms Dyke has “actively promoted veganism” as a way of helping “reduce emissions from animal agriculture”.
The dossier claims that the council’s environment strategy, which was developed and led by Ms Dyke, has the aim of promoting plant-based diets and persuading residents to abandon pork and beef.
The Conservatives point out that Ms Dyke has been environmental portfolio holder for South Somerset Council, whose environment web page states that “meat consumption is one of the biggest contributors to the destruction of forests and biodiversity”.
They claim this flies in the face of the economic interests of Somerset and Frome’s rural communities, which rely heavily on animal farming.
They point out that Ms Dyke has also liked the radical Feed our Future campaign on Facebook, which calls for councils and schools to serve only vegan meals.
In one of her monthly newsletters Ms Dyke wrote, regarding World Vegan Day, that “even if you are not vegan, reducing your meat consumption and replacing some days with vegan or vegetarian meals helps”.
Launching her campaign last week, Ms Dyke, who is also the director of a furniture retailer Vintage Ghetto, said: “Our hardworking farmers are under the cosh from the botched trade deal. I am from a farming family myself, and I understand the dynamics involved, and hope to stand up for them.”
The party also points out that not only was South Somerset District Council’s environment strategy passed with Conservative votes, but Rebecca Pow, Conservative MP for Taunton Dean, also met with Extinction Rebellion at the same event attended by Ms Dyke.
A Lib Dem spokesman said: “This is an embarrassing attempt by the Conservatives to distract from their dire record of slashing support for farmers and undercutting them through botched trade deals.
“Sarah Dyke is proud to be from a local farming family and has used her council role to encourage people to buy high-quality, locally sourced meat.
“As Somerton and Frome’s next MP she would bang the drum tirelessly for local farmers who have been left without a voice for far too long.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/environment/.title: Labour donor and Just Stop Oil backer plots ‘eco-curriculum’ across 12,000 schools
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/environment/.subtitle: Multi-millionaire Dale Vince, a new-age traveller turned ‘green industrialist’, is plotting to ‘green up the national curriculum’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/environment/.text:
A multi-millionaire bankrolling Just Stop Oil protests is plotting the rollout of an “eco-curriculum” across 12,000 UK schools after successful trials across the country.
Dale Vince, a new-age traveller turned “green industrialist”, wants to embed environmental considerations across the curriculum from primary school age.
Children should be taught about “focusing on the energy we use, the way we travel, what we eat and the importance of making room for nature”, according to plans set out in the annual report of Mr Vince’s charitable foundation.
Trials of “greening up the national curriculum” were implemented across 15 primary schools and 10 secondary schools last year. And by the 2022 school year more than 100 schools were “engaging” with literature and other educational tools provided by Mr Vince’s “Ministry of Eco Education”.
Filings with the Charities Commission by the Green Britain Foundation read: “Young people developed a deeper connection with nature and increased knowledge and understanding of the climate and nature emergency.
“Young people experienced increased positive engagement with the local community. Teachers felt more supported and confident to teach education for sustainability.
“Throughout the year the Ministry of Eco Education actively sought relationships to build the scope of the curriculum as well as enlist more schools to take part.”
Mr Vince and the Ministry of Eco Education now wants to extend and adapt the curriculum for a secondary school audience, with plans to reach 10,000 primary and 2,000 Secondary schools by 2025.
So-called “pioneer schools” include Minchinhampton Academy in Stroud, Wycliffe College in the Cotswolds, and St John’s in Marlborough. Paul the “radical geographer” is listed on the Ministry of Eco Education’s website as a leading advocate.
Vince, the founder of electricity supplier Ecotricity, hit the headlines last week by pledging to double any donations to Just Stop Oil over a 48 hour period despite a growing backlash against the group and its attempts to ruin sporting and social events.
In an email to Just Stop Oil supporters on Wednesday, he said: “I was on the front page of Monday’s Daily Mail and Radio 4 this morning for supporting Just Stop Oil, like that’s a crime or something.
“Along with thousands of others, I am proud to donate vital funds to the cause.
“I’m inviting you to join me in supporting the brave people who are currently slow marching, causing disruption and risking their freedom to save us from the climate crisis.
“If you give a donation in the next 48 hours I will match it, pound for pound.
“Winning this argument is all that matters.
“The ordinary people powering Just Stop Oil need our support to keep on doing what they are doing so effectively - and ultimately bring about the change we all demand.”
The self-styled “econaut” has an estimated net worth of more than £100 million after founding Ecotricity, a green energy provider.
But the energy tycoon’s green credentials and Labour donations were not enough to prevent a recent Ministry of Eco Education from falling victim to trade union industrial action.
“Due to the forthcoming train strikes we’ve had to postpone the London Climate Teacher Gathering. We’re hoping to reschedule for July and will keep everyone updated with a new date,” the organisation tweeted.
He has also sought to transform Forest Green Rovers, which will next season play in England’s fourth tier of professional football after being relegated in 2022/23 from League One.
The club offers vegan pies, jerseys made from coffee granules and fertiliser made with the urine of away fans.
The United Nations has said Forest Green Rovers are the world’s first carbon-neutral football club. Global football body Fifa says the club is “the greenest team in the world”.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Keir Starmer: I’ll scrap ban on new onshore wind farms
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: Labour leader fires starting gun on ‘race’ to build more turbines as he vows to ‘throw everything’ at net zero
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Sir Keir Starmer will scrap the ban on new onshore wind farms as one of his first acts in Downing Street if Labour wins the next election.
The opposition leader will vow to “throw everything” at his net zero agenda by firing the starting gun on a “race” to build more turbines across the country.
He will unveil plans to tear up planning laws and halve the length of time it takes for projects to be approved from two years to less than 12 months.
During a speech in Scotland on Monday, he will tell voters they would save hundreds of pounds on their bills under his vision to make Britain a “clean energy superpower”.
Labour says it plans to lift the de facto ban on new wind farms in England, introduced by the Tories in 2012, within its “first months” in power.
But he will make the address following more accusations of “flip-flopping” after he watered down plans to end new North Sea oil and gas projects.
“We can cut bills, create jobs and provide energy security for Britain – that’s what a Labour government will deliver,” Sir Keir will tell an audience in Scotland.
“We’ve got to roll up our sleeves and start building things, run towards the barriers – the planning system, the skills shortages, the investor confidence, the grid.
“If the status quo isn’t good enough – we must find the reforms that can restart our engine.
“I’m not going to accept a situation where our planning system means it takes 13 years to build an offshore wind farm.”
He will add: “We’re going to throw everything at this: planning reform, procurement, long-term finance, R&D, a strategic plan for skills and supply chains.
“We’ve got to seize the new opportunities. This is the race of our lifetime and the prize is real.”
Labour’s energy plan, set to be published on Monday, will formally commit to reversing the onshore wind ban within its first year in power.
But a source close to Sir Keir said he plans to go much faster and bring legislation to the House of Commons within months, adding: “We are going to push on with it ASAP.”
Sir Keir has vowed to reduce the planning process for putting up new turbines “from years to months” and to double output from onshore wind by 2030.
The decade-long ban has added £182 per year to the typical family’s bills by making Britain more reliant on expensive imported energy, he will claim.
Labour has pledged to create a net zero electricity grid by 2030.
Sir Keir’s speech will come after he was criticised by the Tories and some within his own party for watering down two of his key green energy pledges.
He has softened his vow to end all new North Sea oil and gas projects after it came under fire from the unions for putting thousands of jobs at risk.
The announcement comes after Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor, admitted the party’s flagship Green Prosperity Plan is being delayed.
Labour had pledged to spend £28 billion a year on climate-friendly policies but has now said it will not reach that target until it has been in power for at least two and a half years.
Esther McVey, a former Conservative cabinet minister, said on Twitter:
Sir Keir will also attack the SNP for failing to deliver on its clean energy pledges, saying his plan will ensure there is “British power for British jobs” and bolster the union.
He will announce that GB Energy, a new state-owned energy company which Labour plans to set up, would have its headquarters in Scotland.
Under the proposals, residents of communities that host green energy production such as wind farms will be rewarded with money off their bills.
Councils will also be required to proactively identify areas of land that can be turned over for the generation of renewable electricity.
Anas Sarwar, the Scottish Labour leader, has confirmed the party will now allow any new oil and gas licences that are approved by the Tories before it takes power to go ahead.
“We cannot shut off oil and gas, and oil and gas will be a significant part of our energy industry for decades to come,” he told Times Radio.
Grant Shapps, the Energy Security and Net Zero Secretary, told The Telegraph: “Time and again Labour have proven they just can’t be trusted with our economy and our energy security.
“By surrendering to Just Stop Oil’s guerrilla tactics, Keir Starmer is admitting that Labour will decimate the economy, put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk and undermine everything we have done to get bills falling.”
A Conservative Party spokesman added that the proposals would “weaken the UK’s energy security, making us more dependent on Putin”.
Offshore Energies UK, the industry body, has warned Labour’s plan would create 45,000 job losses and lead to a 60 per cent drop in domestic oil and gas production.
The package of reforms being outlined by Sir Keir is seen as vital to making Britain’s electricity grid carbon-free by 2030.
Industry insiders view this goal as extremely challenging, with one boss of a major power generator saying it would be “virtually impossible”.
However, constraints on the planning system and the grid connection queuing process are seen as key bottlenecks.
Under the “first come, first serve” system, developers of solar farms and battery storage projects have been told they may have to wait until the 2030s for their projects to be hooked up to the grid – even though they only take a few years to build.
This has encouraged firms to “pay and spray” applications in different areas to increase their chances of success, clogging up the queue with speculative projects that are going nowhere.
A Labour source said the party would “rip up the queue system” for grid connections, replacing it with a “use it or lose it” process that forces developers to show progress or forfeit their application.
Meanwhile, the current planning process can force companies to carry out a plethora of environmental studies for renewable energy projects, even though other developers have already done similar work for other projects nearby – wasting time and money.
But Labour will pledge to require councils to set aside land for such schemes and investigate ways to allow offshore wind companies to be able to take advantage of existing environmental data to speed up project approvals.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/opera/what-t.title: Glyndebourne’s enchanting new star Liv Redpath on why opera isn’t just for the rich
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/opera/what-t.subtitle: The 31-year-old American soprano, soon to make her UK debut at Glyndebourne, on discipline, class diversity and playing mercurial women
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/opera/what-t.text:
Arriving at Glyndebourne the morning after Just Stop Oil protesters noisily disrupted a performance at the opera house, there’s a surprisingly eerie calm – no added security, no watchful police, just the evidence from the active wind turbine nearby of how misguided it was to target this most sustainable of opera houses. No-one wants to labour discussing the incident. Glyndebourne put out a simple statement the night before, stating that the police had been informed, but the clear sense now is that it’s over, and the focus is on moving forward to the next production. The choice revival of the Glyndebourne summer is Peter Hall’s wonderful, classic production of Benjamin Britten’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, which dates back to 1981 and puts the cast in Elizabethan dress. It is the opera house’s second-oldest production still in their repertory. And, in a treat for fans of vintage Glyndebourne, the oldest production of all – the famous 1975 version of The Rake’s Progress featuring David Hockney’s designs – also returns this year.
The Britten opera features the latest Glyndebourne discovery (the opera house is known for spotting the big stars of the future), American soprano Liv Redpath, 31, who sings Titania. A sensational international career is opening up for this brilliant coloratura soprano, who has been described by critics as “enchanting”, a “revelation”, and with a voice that “penetrates the air”.  After successes in Europe and the United States, she is making her UK debut here on her way to the demanding role of Lucia in Donizetti’s Lucia di Lammermoor at the Royal Opera next year.
While Lucia, with its famously difficult mad scene, will use the full range of her stratospherically high-voiced soprano, the role of Titania is much more part of an ensemble cast, interacting with – among others – the young fairies, played by children who this season including Glyndebourne’s own Bacchus Christie, the eight-year-old son of Gus Christie and Danielle de Niese.
Redpath had an unusual route into the operatic world – she knew she wanted to be a singer since she sang Gretel in Hansel and Gretel at the age of 14. “I just remember when that show ended, not only did I do well, but I felt this incredible rush of knowing myself. That was just it for me,” she says. “But I wanted a kind of depth to the way I went about this career”. So she took what has been a rather British direction for musicians, and went to Harvard College to read English, while spending all her spare time making music.
“When I was there I sang 12 roles, including Titania. I would never have got that in an undergraduate music programme,” she adds. Then she went on to Juilliard, and became a member of the Los Angeles Opera young artist programme.
The roles came fast and mainly high, based on her remarkable top vocal range, but it isn’t something she uses for all her roles. “I don’t always want to be alone in a small bel canto cast, just five of us with our own arias. Here [in A Midsummer Night’s Dream] it’s more of a team show, and we’re working with kids in these scenes who will never forget the experience they are having.
“But Titania is mercurial, so in this opera I get to do whatever extremes seem to work for me! So far I have played quite a few of the ladies who go crazy and release something else deep in themselves.” She first sang Lucia in Germany, and then in a ‘crazy’ production by Australian director Simon Stone in Los Angeles.
Redpath seems totally driven and committed to the operatic life – she even spent the pandemic period learning new roles she might sing one day. In a transatlantic link-up, she has now become the partner of leading English counter-tenor Iestyn Davies, and they will be able both to appear in A Midsummer Night’s Dream in Atlanta next year, where Davies will sing Oberon.
What of the complaint that opera is just expensive indulgence for the rich? “No, no, it’s so great what [director] Barrie Kosky achieved at the Komische Oper in Berlin, where he got people coming in just off the street, cheap tickets, all a casual part of the flow of life. And when I talk to my colleagues, they are not from privileged backgrounds, they’re ordinary people who maybe had the great fortune like I did to be blessed with a wonderful piano teacher from the age of three.”
Any preferences between opera in the US and Europe? “Coming from the US I have found a lot of freedom in Europe where the houses are smaller and my voice can lift over the orchestra”, she says. “ I’ve learned things I can now take back to the US scene.”
Hearteningly for a singer with roots in a 19th-century repertory, she has developed a passion for contemporary work through an association with singer/conductor Barbara Hannigan, and among her wished-for roles for the future is the one that Hannigan premiered in George Benjamin’s great opera Written on Skin.
In everything from Mahler’s Fourth Symphony filmed with Gustavo Dudamel at the Hollywood Bowl, to Beethoven’s Missa solemnis at the Aix Festival this summer, Redpath is working her way through a huge repertory.
But she insists that deep reflection is at the heart of her singing. “I’ve been lucky to see the fruits of self-discipline!” she says. “But in those silent moments on stage where you just take a deep breath and do it, it’s important to know who you are.”
A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Glyndebourne, opens July 1 and runs until August 22. Tickets

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.title: Watch: Furious scaffolders shove Just Stop Oil protesters out of road
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.subtitle: Four activists blocked traffic on a busy street by Pall Mall on Thursday, refusing to let a build-up of lorries pass
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.text:
A pair of furious scaffolders rugby-tackled Just Stop Oil (JSO) protesters blocking traffic on a central London road.
Four JSO activists in high-visibility orange jackets stood in the middle of a busy road by Pall Mall on Thursday, refusing to let a build-up of heavy goods lorries pass as part of a coordinated set of marches across the capital.
Two scaffolders exasperated at the holdup tackled the protestors to the pavement, with one handling three activists at once, while the other confiscated a cardboard picket sign.
Footage showed the remaining demonstrator subjected to a rugby-style tackle by a scaffolder onto the bonnet of a parked white van, and then removed from the road altogether.
The workmen looked palpably irked by the stunt before bringing it to an abrasive conclusion, with the campaigners making no attempt to further obstruct traffic.
Climate activists marched through roads in Chelsea, Hammersmith, and Westminster, on Thursday holding signs which read: “New Oil = Murder” and “we won’t die quietly”.
The Metropolitan Police issued a Section 12 order in all three areas which instructed the protesters to move onto the pavement.
But the order was flouted by eco-activists in several areas, with some members of the public deciding to force them from the roads or find ways around them.
One woman could be heard pleading with the protesters that she needed to pass to get to hospital.
She drove around activists who did not make way but told her to drive slowly, according to Mail Online.
JSO activists were joined by the millionaire Labour donor Dale Vince who posted a picture of himself marching among them outside the Palace of Westminster. Thursday’s protest marks the seventh week of JSO slow-march protests in London.
By way of explanation for this morning’s demonstration, JSO tweeted: “No one likes being disrupted, but also no one likes their government actively planning genocide.”
The Metropolitan Police said in a statement: “We are aware of an incident on Pall Mall at 08:05hrs, where members of the public intervened with a group of protesters slow walking along the road.
“Officers attended the scene and spoke with the protesters where no allegations of a crime were made. No arrests were made.
“We would urge the public not to intervene or take matters into their own hands, but to call the police, let us know where the incident is and we will get to the scene quickly.
“A Section 12 condition was issued to this group at 08:20hrs and by 08:22hrs they moved onto the pavement.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.title: Just Stop Oil protesters halt opera performance with confetti bomb
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.subtitle: Three protesters purchased tickets to Glyndebourne, East Sussex, and began protest an hour into the performance
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters halted an opera performance at Glyndebourne on Thursday afternoon by setting off a confetti bomb and blowing an air horn.
Three protesters purchased tickets for Dialogues des Carmelites at the opera house in East Sussex and, an hour into the performance, leapt from their seats and began shouting.
Audience members booed and shouted: “Disgraceful!” before the protesters were removed from the auditorium. The performance resumed around 20 minutes later, and no arrests were made.
The disruption followed a protest last month at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show, where three activists released orange powder paint in one of the gardens, and another at the World Snooker Championship in April.
A spokesman for Glyndebourne said: “We are very sorry to everyone whose visit was affected by the protest action.
“Our highest priority was the safety and security of everyone on site, and we would like to thank our staff and performers, whose calm and professional response kept everyone safe and disruption to a minimum.
“At approximately 5.31pm, today’s performance of Poulenc’s Dialogues des Carmelites was disrupted by three protesters who let off a confetti bomb, blew an air horn and started shouting. The stage was immediately cleared and within less than a minute ushers had peacefully escorted the protesters from the theatre.
“The audience remained inside the theatre and were provided with regular updates and, following a 21-minute delay, the opera restarted at approximately 5.52pm.
“We have formally reported the incident to the police, but the police were not on site and no arrests were made.”
It is unclear why the protesters chose Glyndebourne, which prides itself on its environmental credentials. The opera house has committed to halve direct carbon emissions by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050.
In 2012, to the dismay of some locals who argued that it was spoiling an area of outstanding natural beauty, Glyndebourne installed a 67-metre wind turbine that was officially unveiled by Sir David Attenborough.
Glyndebourne said at the time that the turbine “provides a visual reminder to us all to do all we can to tackle climate change”.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.title: Just Stop Oil back on London streets despite tougher new protest regulations
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.subtitle: The passing of tighter laws did not deter the group from demonstrating across London
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/06.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters were back out in force on the streets of central London on Wednesday after measures to tackle protests were approved by the House of Lords on Tuesday night.
Environmental activists turned up at Westminster Bridge, London Bridge and Tower Bridge, as well as Vauxhall Bridge Road in Pimlico, Kennington Road in Lambeth and Blackfriars Road in Southwark.
Earlier, the group’s members also demonstrated at four locations across West London: the A40 at Savoy Circus in East Acton; North End Road in West Kensington; Shepherds Bush Road in Hammersmith; and Chiswick Roundabout in Gunnersbury.
In footage filmed by the protesters, a man leading one of the protest groups is arrested after a short discussion with a police officer.
As he is handcuffed and taken to the side of the road, a pedestrian walking past appears to take issue with the protesters.
She says: “People, this is not right. People have to work, they have things to do in their lives.”
In another clip, filmed on the A40, tense scenes were seen as protesters urged each other to “keep walking” while motorists sounded horns behind them.
Around a dozen protesters carrying Just Stop Oil placards also slow-marched across Westminster Bridge towards central London’s Parliament Square.
Within minutes, two police vans arrived and officers explained the new regulations.
They were asked to move to the pavement where they were told it was “fine” to continue their protest.
After polite conversations – with one officer explaining it was a “final warning” – they complied.
The Lords voted through the new regulations on Tuesday evening despite an attempt by Green Party peer Baroness Jones to block them.
The regulations lower the threshold for what kind of protest activity is considered “serious disruption”.
The new law follows last month’s passage of the Public Order Act, legislation designed to strengthen police powers to clamp down on protests judged to be disruptive.
